## 2026-10-31 · The ingress target architecture: an edge network per installed stack, the published ports on one named network, host ingress as two bindings

### DEC-075

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-31 · refines DEC-063 · depends on DEC-064 · area: network
- **Parts:** .1 an edge network per installed stack is the default for a new installation; the shared `proxy-public` stays a documented choice · .2 `proxy-public` carries Traefik's published ports, named by `gw_priority` · .3 host ingress is two bind variables, one per address family; no network mode · .4 IPv6-only means no public IPv4 ingress; a host without IPv4 egress is a prerequisite list; an IPv6-only Docker network is out of scope
- **Implementation:** .2 implemented 2026-10-31 (step 2: `gw_priority: 100` on `public`, the gateway-endpoint checks in core/traefik/ops/scripts/check-published-family.py, the Compose minimum in validate.sh) · .1 implemented 2026-10-31 (step 5: `EDGE_NETWORKS` in core/traefik/.env rendered into config/edge-networks.yml, `name: ${TRAEFIK_NETWORK}` in every stack, the label check in validate.sh, check-structure.py `network-name`, core/traefik/docs/edge-networks.md) · .3 implemented 2026-11-01 (step 7: `TRAEFIK_BIND_V4` and `TRAEFIK_BIND_V6` rendered into config/published-ports.yml, one block per family, an empty variable publishing nothing; neither variable with a default; dual-stack the example's default; docker-compose.yml and network-dual-stack.yml without ports; the nine known unbound stacks on a required `*_BIND` variable, `KNOWN_UNBOUND_PORTS` removed) · implemented 2026-10-31 (step 1, the guards) → scripts/ci/check-structure.py `missing-network-label` and `port-no-host-address`, the subnet check in core/traefik/ops/scripts/validate.sh, scripts/ci/test_traefik_render_identity.py
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_check_structure.py, scripts/ci/test_traefik_published_ports.py, scripts/ci/test_traefik_render_identity.py · review — docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md §4 (a throwaway daemon, IPv4 only: T1–T11) · host — open: the endpoint of the IPv6 ports, the external exposure test, the migration of a shared installation
- **Inputs:** docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md; issue #129; PR #272

The ingress audit of 2026-10-31 (`docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md`)
measured two things the architecture had assumed. Containers on one Docker network
reach each other's ports directly, so on the shared `proxy-public` a compromised web
container reaches every other backend without passing a router position; on separate
networks it reaches nothing (Docker's bridge isolation, measured on Engine 29.9). And
Docker maps Traefik's published ports to its address on the first of its networks in
Compose order — `crowdsec-security`, not `proxy-public` — unless `gw_priority` names
one.

**Decision.** For a new installation every stack has its own edge network, holding
Traefik and the stack's web container; `app-internal` stays as it is. `render.sh`
derives the edge networks from the stacks that are installed and renders them into
Traefik's Compose configuration, as it renders the Cloudflare ranges; the stack's
`TRAEFIK_NETWORK` names the network and the label `traefik.docker.network` is
mandatory. `proxy-public` remains the network that carries the published ports, set by
`gw_priority`, and remains the shared network for an installation that chooses it — with
the stated consequence that its members reach one another. Host ingress is two bind
variables, `TRAEFIK_BIND_V4` and `TRAEFIK_BIND_V6`, each a host address or empty; the
network behind them is dual-stack for a new installation. There is no network mode.

**Conditions.** A step changes what it says it changes and nothing else —
`scripts/ci/test_traefik_render_identity.py` holds the rendered configuration of the
IPv4-only and the dual-stack shape against v0.9.5 outside the regions a decision moved.
Before v1.0 a breaking change with a migration is preferred to a compatibility gate
(DEC-076, amended). Adding an edge network costs a recreate of Traefik (about two
seconds, measured); a stack whose network Traefik does not join is unreachable and the
log says nothing, so the label rule and the derived list are what make the default
safe. The IPv4 address pool of a default daemon holds 32 user networks (measured) — two
per stack plus the three of `core/traefik`, so fourteen stacks before
`default-address-pools` is set.

**The installed stacks are an explicit list (step 5, 2026-10-31).** `EDGE_NETWORKS` in
`core/traefik/.env` names the edge network of every installed stack — the stack's
`TRAEFIK_NETWORK`, `<project>-edge` as the examples ship it. A list the operator writes
is the signal: the presence of an `.env` says nothing about a stack being deployed, and
reading the running projects would make the render depend on what happens to run.
render.sh writes the list into `config/edge-networks.yml`, a Compose file that
`COMPOSE_FILE` applies next to docker-compose.yml, as the dual-stack overlay already is;
Traefik creates each network and joins it, the stack declares it external. Unset stops
the render like `TRUSTED_RANGES`; `scripts/migrate-traefik-env.sh` adds the line. The
examples' default moves to the edge network; an installation's `.env` keeps
`proxy-public` until it chooses. Mailpit and GreenMail ship on the shared network,
because being reached by every other stack is what they are for.

**The bindings are rendered per family (step 7, 2026-11-01).** A fixed port line in a
Compose file cannot be left out when its variable is empty, so `docker-compose.yml`
publishes nothing and `render.sh` writes the two bindings into
`config/published-ports.yml`, which `COMPOSE_FILE` applies like the edge networks:
an empty variable publishes nothing for its family, and neither has a default —
`render.sh` and `validate.sh` refuse `TRAEFIK_BIND_V4` unset, so a missing line never
becomes `0.0.0.0`. `.env.example` ships dual-stack (`0.0.0.0`, `[::]`, the overlay),
DEC-063's default for a new installation. `render.sh` refuses an IPv6 binding without `network-dual-stack.yml`, the overlay with
`TRAEFIK_BIND_V6` unset, and a `COMPOSE_FILE` without the rendered file;
`scripts/migrate-traefik-env.sh` completes `COMPOSE_FILE`, writes `0.0.0.0` where
`TRAEFIK_BIND_V4` was missing and keeps `[::]` for an installation that applied the
overlay. The nine stacks the audit listed bind each
published port to a required `*_BIND` variable, IPv4 as shipped. The IPv6 endpoint,
an IPv6-only host and the bound stacks over IPv6 are host proofs of step 8.

**Refines DEC-063.** The goals stand — dual-stack for a new installation, IPv4-only and
IPv6-only supported, no automatic change, no security lost by the default. The three
operating modes become bind decisions: `ipv4-only` is `TRAEFIK_BIND_V6` empty,
`ipv6-only` is `TRAEFIK_BIND_V4` empty. What an IPv6-only host needs for its outbound
connections is the prerequisite list in the audit (§3.4), not a mode; an IPv6-only
Docker network — backends listening on `::` only — is out of scope.

## 2026-10-31 · `access-trusted` replaces `access-lan`: no address class is trusted by default

### DEC-076

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-31 · refines DEC-064 · area: reverse-proxy
- **Parts:** .1 `access-lan` and `access-lan-vpn` are retired names — a breaking change with a migration, no second rendering · .2 `access-trusted` and `access-trusted-vpn` admit the ranges `TRUSTED_RANGES` declares, rendered as a list; empty admits nobody; unset stops the render · .3 a declared range that overlaps the VPN range or a Docker subnet is refused · .4 an integration that calls an application back does so over a Docker network with the application's own setting for it, never through a closed route
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-10-31 (step 3) → core/traefik/ops/templates/dynamic/model.yml.tmpl, core/traefik/ops/scripts/render.sh (`ACCESS_TRUSTED_RANGES_YAML`, unset refused), core/traefik/ops/scripts/validate.sh (the range checks, `access-lan*` retired in the rendered file), core/traefik/.env.example (`TRUSTED_RANGES=""`), scripts/migrate-traefik-env.sh (the rename, the line added to the core .env), scripts/ci/check-structure.py and check-prose.py (`access-lan*` retired), fifteen stack examples, apps/seafile and apps/seafile-pro `onlyoffice-callback.yml`, the Nextcloud and Seafile READMEs, docs/standards/traefik-security.md
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_traefik_render_identity.py (everything but position 1 unchanged), scripts/ci/test_traefik_model.py (the ranges, the refusals, the retired name in a rendered file), scripts/ci/test_migrate_traefik_env.py (the rename, the added line), scripts/ci/test_check_structure.py (the retired name) · review — docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md §4, T2c and T8 · host — open: a tailnet client and a declared LAN client against each policy, over both families
- **Inputs:** docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md §2 and §4; issue #129; docs/standards/traefik-security.md "Known limitation"

`access-lan` admits RFC 1918 and `fc00::/7`. Both contain every Docker subnet, and the
second contains Tailscale's range: a tailnet client over IPv6 passes a LAN-only policy,
and — measured 2026-10-31 — a compromised container on any network Traefik joins passes
it by sending another stack's host name to Traefik's address on its own network. An
edge network per stack does not change that (T2c); only the policy does.

**Decision.** A new installation gets no LAN class. An operator who wants one declares
the ranges — the LAN's own prefixes, IPv4 and IPv6 — in `TRUSTED_RANGES`; `render.sh`
renders them as the list of `access-trusted`, and `validate.sh` refuses a range that
contains the VPN range or a Docker subnet of the daemon. No list is computed; what is
trusted is what was written. `access-vpn` stays: the VPN range is a property of the
host's tunnel interface, not a judgement about the device, and the host firewall's
anti-spoofing rule (DEC-078) is what keeps it so over both families.

**Breaking, with a migration (amended 2026-10-31).** The first cut kept a second
rendering for an `.env` without the variable. The maintainer withdrew that: before
v1.0 a breaking change that simplifies the model is preferred to a gate, a second
shape and tests for a retired security model. `access-lan` and `access-lan-vpn` are
retired names like `acc-*`; an `.env` without `TRUSTED_RANGES` stops `render.sh` and
`validate.sh` with the migration named. `scripts/migrate-traefik-env.sh --all` adds the
line to `core/traefik/.env` and renames the policy in every stack's `.env`.

**Integrations that call back.** A container never reaches a closed route through the
proxy any more, and no exception admits one. What the LAN class used to carry by
accident is carried on purpose: over a Docker network the two containers share, with
the setting the application has for it — Nextcloud's OnlyOffice connector
(`StorageUrl`, `DocumentServerInternalUrl`) and Collabora app (`wopi_url`,
`wopi_callback_url`), SeaDoc's `SEAHUB_SERVICE_URL`, which the stack already sets.
Seafile hands OnlyOffice no internal address — the document fetch on `/seafhttp/files/`
(a one-hour access token) and the save callback (acted on for an issued document key
only; seahub verifies no JWT there) — so the stack carries an opt-in file with routes
for those two paths; a Document Server on another host is trusted by its address in
`TRUSTED_RANGES` instead. Verified against seahub 13.0 and master, 2026-10-31. Nextcloud's own setup checks call its public name and report failures on a
closed route; the README says so.

## 2026-10-31 · The auth position states a posture; `auth-none` is a statement, not a gap

### DEC-077

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-31 · refines DEC-064 · area: identity
- **Parts:** .1 `auth-none` means no additional authentication at the proxy — the application's own login, or a public service by design · .2 every stack's `.env.example` states its posture beside `APP_TRAEFIK_AUTH`: `app-login`, `public`, `basic`, `forward-auth` or `none` · .3 `none` — no login anywhere — requires a closed access policy and a stated reason · .4 no login layer is forced; Traefik's `basicAuth` is the built-in gate where a web interface holds data and no identity provider exists
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-10-31 (step 4) → every `.env.example` (`# auth posture:` above the auth variable), scripts/ci/check-structure.py (`auth-posture`), docs/standards/traefik-security.md, docs/standards/traefik-labels.md, docs/standards/env-structure.md, apps/_reference, the stacks without a login: apps/ollama, apps/homepage, apps/dashy, apps/heimdall (basicAuth from `APP_BASIC_AUTH_USERS`), apps/mailpit (`MP_UI_AUTH_FILE`), apps/it-tools, apps/httpbin, apps/whoami, apps/greenmail, monitoring/gatus (`none`, closed)
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_check_structure.py `AuthPosture` (the rule, and every catalogue example states a posture) · review — docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md §4, T4a–T4c · host — open: a real outpost; the five gates on a host
- **Inputs:** docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md §2.3 and §4

Of 109 catalogue stacks, 106 carry `auth-none@file` and none carries forward-auth by
default; nine have no login of their own and are reached through `access-vpn` alone.
The lab measured both sides of the position (T4): a forward-auth gate deletes every
client copy of its response headers and lets nothing through without a 2xx from the
auth server; a route with `auth-none` passes a client's `X-authentik-username` to the
backend unchanged.

**Decision.** The position keeps its values and gains a stated posture per stack, so
that `auth-none` reads as what it is. An application with its own sufficient login
needs no further gate. An application with no login that is stateless and holds no data
may stay behind a closed access policy with the reason written down. An application
with no login that holds data or capability — a mail catcher, a model runtime, a
dashboard with API keys — gets a gate: `basicAuth` from Traefik or forward-auth from
the identity provider, whichever the installation has. Authentik stays the reference
implementation and is required by none of this.

**Decided one by one (step 4, 2026-10-31).** The posture is a comment line directly
above the variable, `# auth posture: <posture> — <reason>`, read by CI — no variable,
no rendering, nothing an installation has to migrate. Of the nine stacks named above,
Homarr has had its own login since 1.0 and is `app-login`. Mailpit has its own gate,
`MP_UI_AUTH_FILE`, which covers the UI and the API and so also holds against a
container that reaches port 8025 directly; the stack now ships it from `.secrets/`
(`app-login`). Ollama, Homepage, Dashy and Heimdall have none that holds — Dashy's is
client-side, Heimdall's users are off until created — and ship Traefik's basicAuth from
`APP_BASIC_AUTH_USERS`, the pattern of `apps/paperless-gpt` (`basic`). whoami, httpbin
and it-tools are stateless and stay `none` behind their closed policy with the reason
written. The sweep found two more without a login: GreenMail (a test fixture with
authentication disabled by design) and Gatus (a status page; its own basic auth or
forward-auth adds a login) — both `none` behind a closed policy, with the reason.
vLLM's API key covers `/v1` only, which its posture line says.

## 2026-10-31 · Exposure is derived and shown; protection layers are classed, never scored

### DEC-078

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-31 · depends on DEC-075 · area: host
- **Parts:** .1 no exposure variable: `validate.sh` derives `direct`, `proxied` or `private` from the bind variables and `TRAEFIK_FORWARDED_PROXY`, and never presents it as measured reachability · .2 the mandatory invariants are what the blueprint controls inside the host; a host firewall ruleset is rendered and recommended, CrowdSec, Cloudflare and Authentik stay optional, and a missing optional layer is named with its residual risk, never counted as an error · .3 an exposure test run from outside the host records a marker that `validate.sh --strict` requires for a public binding · .4 management access has two independent paths, identity by key, and no automatically filled rule reaches the management interface
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-11-01 (step 6) → core/traefik/ops/scripts/exposure-profile.sh (the derivation), core/traefik/ops/scripts/validate.sh (the profile, the layers, the marker), core/traefik/ops/scripts/render.sh (config/host/ingress.nft), scripts/exposure-test.sh, core/traefik/ops/host-files.manifest, core/traefik/docs/host-firewall.md, docs/standards/deployment-lifecycle.md
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_traefik_exposure.py (the derivation, the layers, the marker, `nft -c` on every rendered profile, the test script against a stub) · host — open: the ruleset loaded on a host, the management gates over both families, the second path used once, the exposure test against a real host
- **Inputs:** docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md §2.4, §3 and §5; core/crowdsec/docs/firewall-bouncer.md §The management-plane invariant

A derived profile says what the configuration intends to expose. NAT, a router, a
hoster firewall or the absence of any of them decide what is reachable, and only a
request from outside the host measures that. The two are kept apart by name and by
mechanism: the profile is printed, the measurement is recorded.

**Decision.** The blueprint guarantees what it controls: only Traefik is published and
only on named addresses, backends are never published, networks are isolated as
decided, no address class is trusted, headers are sanitised by sender, forward-auth
fails closed, the management path does not run through Traefik or Docker. Everything
a host needs beyond that is a layer: a host firewall where no upstream firewall
exists or where Cloudflare fronts the origin, CrowdSec for detection, an identity
provider for weak logins, Authenticated Origin Pulls or a tunnel behind Cloudflare.
`validate.sh --strict` lists the layers for the derived profile — present, absent with
the risk it leaves — and requires the exposure marker for a public binding. Nothing
optional is a defect by its absence; nothing absent is silent.

**Implemented (step 6, 2026-11-01).** The profile: `direct` when a binding is
`0.0.0.0`, `[::]` or a global address with no trusted proxy, `proxied` when such a
binding sits behind `TRAEFIK_FORWARDED_PROXY=cloudflare`, `private` when every binding
is a loopback, LAN, VPN or link-local address or nothing is published; the IPv6 binding
counts when the dual-stack overlay is applied. The ruleset `config/host/ingress.nft` is
one `nftables` table: input closed except loopback, established, ICMP, the DHCP clients,
Tailscale's port and everything from the VPN ranges; forward policy `accept` with the
anti-spoofing drop for the VPN's IPv6 range on every interface but `VPN_INTERFACE` and,
for `proxied`, the drop of new connections to Traefik's translated ports from anyone
but Cloudflare, the VPN and `TRUSTED_RANGES`. `nft -c` accepts every rendered profile;
a host has not loaded it yet. The exposure test probes 80 and 443 over both families,
the ports that must never answer, and reports SSH without judging it; its marker line
in `config/exposure-verified` names date, target and profile, and `validate.sh`
refuses a marker for another profile. The management requirement is stated in the
layer list and the deployment lifecycle; the second path cannot be checked from the
host.

## 2026-10-23 · The cut ships as v0.9.5 without a reference tag; the documentation follows in four pull requests

### DEC-065

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-23 (amended 2026-10-25: one migration test precedes the tag) · depends on DEC-064 · area: release
- **Parts:** .1 v0.9.5 with a Release page, not v0.10.0 · .2 no pre-cut tag; `1041a02` is the reference commit · .3 records keep the names of their time · .4 the guard against retired names warns, then fails · .5 validate.sh's search of config/host is corrected before the release · .6 one migration test precedes the tag
- **Implementation:** .1 implemented 2026-10-31 (the tag `v0.9.5` on `main` and the Release page; docs/maintenance.md Release Chain step 7 still says a patch tag gets no GitHub Release) · .2 implemented (no tag set) · .3 implemented (the records keep their names) · .4 implemented → `RETIRED_GATE` in scripts/ci/check-prose.py, FAIL since Phase 4.4c (#264) · .5 implemented (#266) · .6 implemented 2026-10-30 (the migration from v0.9.4 on a disposable installation)
- **Verification:** .1 mechanical — `git tag -l v0.9.5`, `gh release view v0.9.5` · .4 mechanical — scripts/ci/test_check_prose.py · .5 mechanical — scripts/ci/test_traefik_entrypoint.py · .6 host — 2026-10-30, a disposable installation of v0.9.4 behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, by core/traefik/docs/middleware-model-migration.md §4: no abort condition met

Decided by the maintainer after Phase 4.3 was accepted, and applied through Phase 4.4
(#262–#264, 2026-10-24).

- **The next version is v0.9.5**, covering the cut and its documentation. The release
  gets a GitHub Release page that names the breaking change and the migration steps;
  the number does not jump to v0.10.0, which stays the measured-resource-limits
  milestone.
- **No pre-cut tag.** `1041a02`, `dev` before the cut, is the reference commit; an
  installation that has not migrated runs v0.9.4, the last release and the rollback
  target.
- **Records stay as written.** A verification record — a dated section or a measured
  line in an `UPSTREAM.md`, the audits, the reviews, the migration document — keeps the
  names of its time; a measurement in current documentation keeps its numbers and names
  the old value as an old-to-new reference. Current instructions say what the files
  ship, and a document that disagreed with a stack's files was corrected to the files.
- **The guard against the retired names warns while the documentation moves and fails
  afterwards** (`RETIRED_GATE` in `scripts/ci/check-prose.py`): WARN from Phase 4.4a,
  FAIL since 4.4c. The exemptions are the record paths, old-to-new context and the
  records above — a dated or verification-headed section of an `UPSTREAM.md` as a
  whole, a measured line on its own — and there is no blanket exemption for
  `UPSTREAM.md`.
- **`validate.sh`'s search of `config/host/`** is corrected before the release and is
  not part of Phase 4 (`tasks.md` §10).
- **One targeted migration test precedes the tag** (added 2026-10-25): the migration from
  v0.9.4 to the model on a disposable installation, by the procedure of the migration
  document's §4 — no production server, no wider test campaign. The proofs its §5 lists
  stay open for a later host session.

## 2026-10-18 · The middleware model as cut: eight decisions (D1–D8)

### DEC-064

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-18 · supersedes DEC-062, DEC-061, DEC-049 · depends on DEC-060 · answers review D1–D8 · area: reverse-proxy
- **Parts:** .1 threat and compression on the entrypoint · .2 four positions on every router · .3 `limit-standard` 125/500 · .4 three header profiles and per-header blocks · .5 one central TLS standard · .6 every router carries the four positions · .7 whole-word names · .8 a hard cut
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-10-23 (#258; prepared #241, #242; documented #262–#264) → core/traefik/ops/templates/dynamic/model.yml.tmpl, core/traefik/ops/templates/traefik.yml.tmpl, docs/standards/traefik-security.md, docs/standards/traefik-labels.md; unreleased, target v0.9.5
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_traefik_model.py, scripts/ci/test_traefik_router_model.py, scripts/ci/check-structure.py (`router-positions`, `retired-name`, `block-order`) · open — host: core/traefik/docs/middleware-model-migration.md §5 · host — the migration from v0.9.4 by §4, 2026-10-30 · .5 open — hot reload of the `default` TLS option unknown, a restart is required
- **Inputs:** docs/audits/traefik-architecture-review-2026-10-17.md §9; core audit RP18

Phase 4 of the core audit, applied 2026-10-22 on `feature/traefik-hard-cut`. The
measurements of 2026-10-18 (a throwaway Traefik v3.7.15 with a file provider only) and
every router's before and after are in
[`../core/traefik/docs/middleware-model-migration.md`](../core/traefik/docs/middleware-model-migration.md).
This supersedes the two entries of 2026-10-15 below where they differ: four positions
on the router instead of six functions, threat and compression on the entrypoint,
`headers-none` as "HSTS only" instead of `headers-hsts-only`.

**D1 — Threat and compression on the entrypoint.** `render.sh` places `threat-crowdsec`
(or `threat-crowdsec-appsec` by its own switch) and `compress` on `websecure`, in front
of every router. HSTS is not placed there: an entrypoint `headers` middleware overwrites
every router header of the same name (measured), and a per-domain extension would be
impossible.

**D2 — Four positions on every router, equal in rank:** access, limit, headers, auth —
each a variable of the stack, no Compose default; an empty variable disables the
router, loudly.

**D3 — `limit-standard` is 125 requests per second with a burst of 500.** The bucket of
200 is retired; `limit-extra-large` is accepted by CI only behind a closed access
policy.

**D4 — Three header profiles and per-header blocks.** `headers-standard`,
`headers-application-owned`, `headers-none`, every one starting with the HSTS base;
`includeSubDomains` and `preload` by the block `hsts-include-subdomains` per host name,
never a default, never `preload` automatically (H2). An application measured to send its
own headers takes `application-owned` plus the single blocks it lacks.

**D5 — One central TLS standard.** The file provider's reserved `default` option, built
from `TLS_DEFAULT_OPTION` (variant A: the routers keep `tls=true`, the entrypoint option
is not used — it reaches no such router, measured). A router names an option only as a
documented exception; two routers of one host name with different options are a CI
error; `core.strictTLSOptions` stays off until the validator has run on every host.

**D6 — Every router, primary or secondary, carries the four positions explicitly.** A
secondary router gets a variable of its own only where its answer differs.

**D7 — Whole-word names.** `access-public|lan|vpn|lan-vpn|blocked`,
`limit-none|standard|extra-large|sync|strict`, `headers-standard|application-owned|none`,
`auth-none|authentik`, `tls-compatible|standard|strict`, `threat-crowdsec[-appsec]`.
The rename of `TAILSCALE_CIDR_*` to `VPN_CIDR_*` is deferred to a change of its own.

**D8 — A hard cut.** The repository replaces the model completely, without aliases;
running servers are migrated one at a time under their own plan; the previous version
stays reproducible by its tag; no production change without its own release.

**Precisions.** Compression exclusions are exact types (octet-stream and png measured as
wasted work); SSE stays compressible. What a migration preserves is the existing proxied
behaviour, not the backend's direct header (Keycloak's HSTS). The office servers keep
the header set their own middleware set, minus the obsolete XSS filter, until measured.
A secondary router keeps the effective value it had wherever the review's value was an
assumption.

## 2026-10-16 · Dual-stack is the default for new installations; IPv4-only and IPv6-only are supported variants

### DEC-063

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-16 (conditional: "a feasibility, limitation and migration-effort assessment of the three modes comes first" — none exists) · supersedes DEC-006 · rejects core D12 ("keep opt-in, state it") · area: network
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-11-01 through DEC-075.3 (step 7): dual-stack is the default of core/traefik/.env.example, IPv4-only and IPv6-only are one bind variable left empty — core/traefik/ops/scripts/render.sh (config/published-ports.yml), core/traefik/network-dual-stack.yml, core/traefik/.env.example; the assessment the condition asked for is docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_traefik_published_ports.py, scripts/ci/test_traefik_published_family.py · host — open: the IPv6 endpoint, an IPv6-only host (step 8)
- **Inputs:** core audit D12; issue #129 (`access-lan` admits the bridge gateway); docs/bugfixes/traefik-ipv6-dualstack-2026-06-19.md

**Addendum 2026-10-31.** The assessment is done ([`../docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md`](../docs/audits/ingress-architecture-2026-10-31.md)) and DEC-075 refines this entry: the goals stand, the three operating modes under one configuration concept do not. Dual-stack is the state of the network that carries the published ports; `ipv4-only` and `ipv6-only` are the two bind variables with one of them empty; what an IPv6-only host needs for its outbound connections is a prerequisite list. Nothing below is withdrawn; the shape of its implementation is DEC-075's.

D12 of the core audit (`docs/audits/core-v1-readiness-2026-10-15.md`). IPv6 is not an
optional extra.

**Decision.** Three operating modes under one configuration concept that covers the
host network, the Docker networks, Traefik and the firewall: `dual-stack`, the default
for new installations; `ipv4-only`, a deliberate alternative; `ipv6-only`, a deliberate
alternative that also serves a host without a public IPv4 address.

**Conditions.** An existing installation is never switched automatically — it gets a
separate, controlled migration path. The dual-stack default reduces no security: access
policies and firewall rules work over both protocols. IPv6-only is checked for outbound
connections, DNS, Docker images and external services. Public host addresses and
internal Docker networks stay apart. The effects on the Docker daemon configuration,
the restarts it needs and existing containers are documented before implementation.
The bridge trust set of issue #129 is handled correctly in every mode.

**Consequence.** A feasibility, limitation and migration-effort assessment of the three
modes comes first; the implementation is released after it. Until then `proxy-public`
stays IPv4-only by default (2026-06, below).

## 2026-10-15 · The Traefik middleware model: six functions, one variable each

### DEC-062

- **Decision:** superseded 2026-10-18 by DEC-064 · answers core D1 · area: reverse-proxy
- **Implementation:** n/a (prepared beside the old names in #241, replaced by the four positions before a release)
- **Verification:** n/a
- **Inputs:** docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md

D1 of the core audit; the design is [`../docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md`](../docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md).

**Decision.** The `sec-*` chains are replaced by six independently chosen functions per
router — threat, access, limit, auth, headers, compress — each a middleware named
`<function>-<variant>` and each set by its own variable. Names decided: `access-public`
and `access-blocked`; `access-vpn`; `threat-crowdsec-appsec`; `headers-hsts-only`;
compression fixed in the label; `HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS` off by default.

**Conditions.** Every protection is kept or exceeded, established against the real
response headers of each affected application before and after — no header is removed
without that pair on record. An existing installation never receives a different
profile without an explicit step: no Compose defaults in the label, a migration script,
an alias check with identical headers and identical `429` behaviour. Names are
understandable and unabbreviated; the default case asks for few decisions.

**Open.** The name of today's bucket of 1000 (`limit-extra-large` proposed), and whether
`headers-standard-frame-self` is created at all — the listmonk measurement decides.

## 2026-10-15 · Cloudflare is a supported operating variant, switched in `.env`

### DEC-060

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-15 (amended 2026-10-17: the `X-Real-Ip` Transform-Rule mechanism dropped, `X-Forwarded-For` with `forwardedHeadersTrustedIPs` shipped — addendum below) · answers core D3 · area: reverse-proxy
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-10-17 (#238, #239) → core/traefik/ops/templates/traefik.yml.tmpl (`forwardedHeaders`), core/traefik/ops/templates/dynamic/crowdsec.yml.tmpl, core/traefik/ops/cloudflare-ips.txt, core/traefik/README.md §Behind Cloudflare
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_traefik_forwarded_proxy.py, scripts/ci/check-cloudflare-ips.py, .github/workflows/cloudflare-ips.yml (weekly) · review — docs/reviews/phase-3-cloudflare-mode-review-2026-10-17.md, docs/reviews/phase-3-cloudflare-mode-review-2-2026-10-17.md, docs/reviews/phase-3-f6-guard-rereview-2026-10-17.md · open — host: core/traefik/README.md "Not verified on a host" (ten checks); the test server was deferred on 2026-10-18
- **Inputs:** core audit C.1 (RP1, RP2); docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md

D3 of the core audit; the mechanism is verified against the Traefik v3.7 source in
[`../docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md`](../docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md), section "Behind Cloudflare — D3".

**Decision.** `TRAEFIK_FORWARDED_PROXY=none|cloudflare` in `core/traefik/.env`, default
`none`; without Cloudflare nothing changes. Closed access policies keep the connecting
address; the limits use `requestHeaderName: X-Real-Ip` together with a Cloudflare
Transform Rule that overwrites `X-Real-Ip` with the connecting client; the CrowdSec
middlewares get `forwardedHeadersTrustedIPs` from the same maintained list as the
entrypoint; the `none` mode trusts no sender. `ipStrategy.depth` is rejected: it yields
an empty address for every direct client.

**Conditions.** One traceable derivation of the client address. Trusted proxies only
from a defined, maintained source — a CI-checked list. No client-supplied address
header taken on trust. Consistent evaluation by access, limits, CrowdSec and logging.
Origin protection documented, so Cloudflare cannot be bypassed. Proof with and without
Cloudflare, over IPv4 and IPv6, on real request paths, before the implementation counts
as done.

**Addendum 2026-10-17 — as shipped (Phase 3, branch `feature/cloudflare-mode`).** The
proposal document is `docs/research/traefik-middleware-proposal-2026-10-15.md` (kept as
record since 2026-10-23). Two parts of the decision above did not survive implementation. The limits do
not use `requestHeaderName: X-Real-Ip`: Cloudflare's Transform Rules cannot modify
`x-real-ip` (or `x-forwarded-for`, `true-client-ip`, `cf-connecting-ip`), and a
header-reading strategy leaves a direct client without an address — `ipAllowList`
refuses it, `rateLimit` shares one bucket. The limits therefore stay on the connecting
address, per edge at the origin, and the per-client limit of a public route is a
Cloudflare rate-limiting rule at the edge. And the CrowdSec middlewares keep the
plugin's default header `X-Forwarded-For` with `forwardedHeadersTrustedIPs`: the first
cut set `forwardedHeadersCustomName: CF-Connecting-IP`, which the independent review
(`docs/reviews/phase-3-cloudflare-mode-review-2026-10-17.md`, F1) showed the plugin
reads from any sender, since Traefik deletes only `X-Forwarded-*`. The condition "no
client-supplied address header taken on trust" is met by the entrypoint deleting
`X-Forwarded-For` from every sender outside the ranges. Trust is bounded by
Cloudflare's network, not by this zone (Workers, other zones, WARP clients); binding it
to the zone — Authenticated Origin Pulls or a Tunnel — is a follow-up. The proof over
IPv4 and IPv6 on a host is open.

## 2026-10-15 · Host-side files are rendered and compared, never installed by the blueprint

### DEC-058

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-15 · answers core D5 · area: host
- **Implementation:** implemented 2026-10-16 (#233) → scripts/host-files.sh (render, check, diff, install-commands), docs/standards/host-files.md, three manifests (core/traefik/ops, core/host-watchdog/ops, backup/borgmatic/ops), `./scripts/overview.sh --host`
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_host_files.py · open — the host checks B1–B6 of docs/host-verification-phase-2.md have not run

D5 of the core audit.

**Decision.** `render.sh` — and the equivalent per stack — writes every host-side file
with the real paths into `<stack>/config/host/`. One uniform check, `overview.sh --host`,
compares each installed file with the rendered one and reports one of four states —
identical, differs, not installed, not checkable — naming the source file and the real
host path, with the diff available before any manual take-over. Installation and
updates stay a separate, controlled manual step.

**Conditions.** No automatic installation or overwrite. File permissions, sensitive
contents and local adaptations are taken into account. Nothing is written outside the
blueprint directory without explicit approval. One procedure for all stacks, no
per-stack special cases.

## 2026-10-15 · Renovate detects upstream releases; nothing is adopted automatically

### DEC-057

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-15 · answers core D6 · rejects stab D5 (delete `renovate.json`) · area: updates
- **Implementation:** not started → renovate.json (committed 2026-09-17, #99); 0 `# renovate:` markers; the App's installation is not visible from the repository
- **Verification:** n/a
- **Inputs:** docs/renovate-proposal.md; core audit UP5 (the manual security-update lane against SECURITY.md's seven days)

D6 of the core audit; it answers the questions of `docs/renovate-proposal.md` and
D5 of the stabilization audit.

**Decision.** Renovate is the central detection of new upstream versions. Every image
pin carries an unambiguous marker; proposals arrive as pull requests and are never
auto-merged; patch and minor updates are grouped, majors come one by one with manual
review; security-relevant updates are recognisable and can be prioritised; Renovate and
the Trivy and security checks complement each other; existing versioning schemes and
deliberately fixed pins are never changed uncontrolled; a proof that every intended pin
is covered, with the list of unsupported exceptions. The configuration is validated and
a test run performed before the automation is switched on. No automatic deployments or
production updates.

Two dialects existed: 52 files with the reference's long-dash headers carrying a layer

## 2026-10-03 · Mail ports are published by the stack, not routed by Traefik

### DEC-050

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-03 · area: reverse-proxy
- **Implementation:** implemented → apps/stalwart/mail.yml (25, 465, 993) and the mail overlays of the two other mail stacks; core/traefik gets no TCP entrypoints
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/check-overlays.py validates each overlay as a deployment variant · n/a — the stacks' evidence is LIFECYCLE.md's

The mail evaluation left two questions for before the first stack: how SMTP and
IMAP are exposed, and where a mail server's certificate comes from. Both are
answered with the first stack, `apps/stalwart`.

**The stack publishes its mail ports, through an opt-in overlay.** `mail.yml`
publishes 25, 465 and 993, as `trapper.yml` does for Zabbix and `derp.yml` for
headscale. `core/traefik` gets no TCP entrypoints: that would publish mail ports
on the proxy of every installation that enables it, and the mail server would
have to trust a PROXY header by source address on a network every routed stack
shares. Port 25 has to be open to the whole internet for mail to arrive, so an
access policy in front of it would have nothing to decide.

**What protects those ports is the mail server, set up by the stack.** The
blueprint's part is to ship the server's own protections switched on and
measured — no relay, authenticated submission, automatic bans with an expiry —
and to say what the operator owns: the firewall, the provider's outbound port
25, DNS and reverse DNS.

**The certificate is stated per stack.** A mail server holds its own; which
sources it supports differs by product, so each README names them. Traefik's
`acme.json` is not mounted into a mail container by default, because it carries
every certificate the proxy has obtained.

**Stalwart runs upstream's image**, with its separately licensed enterprise code
in it and unlocked only by a key — `business/twenty` is the precedent — and mail
servers sit in `apps/`: they serve their own users.

**What would change it.** A stack that needs the client address and cannot get
it on a published port, established on a host.

---

## 2026-10-03 · The rate limits are widened until the Traefik review settles them

### DEC-049

- **Decision:** superseded 2026-10-18 by DEC-064.3 · area: reverse-proxy
- **Implementation:** n/a (was implemented 2026-10-03, #218; replaced by the model's `limit-*` values)
- **Verification:** n/a
- **Inputs:** the first loads of 2026-09-22 and the sync clients' `429` (docs/audits/reverse-proxy-limits-2026-09-23.md)

Sync clients of Seafile and Nextcloud failed with `429` in operation, and the
first loads measured in September — 77 to 291 requests — did not fit the default
burst of 50. The Traefik review owns the real answer: what each chain is for, and
whether static files and sync paths belong under the counter at all. Until it
lands, the limits are wide enough that ordinary use passes.

**What the limit is for stays as the review states it.** It keeps the proxy and
the origin answering while one client asks for a lot; it is not the defence
against password guessing
([`../docs/audits/reverse-proxy-limits-2026-09-23.md`](../docs/audits/reverse-proxy-limits-2026-09-23.md)).
A limit that answers `429` to a first load or to a sync protects nothing and
breaks the application.

**The values.** `rl-soft` 125 requests per second with a burst of 200, from 100
and 50: the bucket refills during a load, and on 2026-09-22 a bucket of 200
answered all 291 requests of the heaviest interface below the `-xl` pair.
`rl-spa` keeps the rate and widens the burst from 200 to 500. `rl-spa-xl` keeps
its bucket of 1000 and its restriction to a closed access policy, and its average
moves from 100 to 125 like the others. `rl-hard`, 20 and 40, is unchanged — it is
chosen where each request is worth slowing down.

**A sync is bounded by the rate, not by the bucket.** The Nextcloud desktop
client runs up to 20 requests in parallel over HTTP/2, the Seafile client three
upload and three download threads with one request per block. The rate is the
parallelism divided by the time one request takes — 400 per second at 20 in
parallel and 50 ms each — so no bucket holds a sync of ten thousand files.
`rl-sync` allows 1000 requests per second, in `sec-2-sync` and `sec-3e-sync`.

**The sync chains are not tied to a closed access policy**, unlike the `-xl`
chains. Nextcloud and Seafile ship `acc-private` and are opened once configured —
an office server calls back over the public name — and their sync endpoints
require credentials.

**No name is removed or renamed.** A deployment that names a chain keeps its
router; `sec-3e-spa` stays although no shipped stack uses it now. The decision
of 2026-09-22 stands: no stack drops to `sec-1` to get past a limit.

**What this does not establish.** The sync figures are read from the clients'
source, not counted on a host; the first run with real clients counts the `429`
in the proxy's access log. And the limit counts per client address: where every
client arrives from one address — a NAT, or the Docker gateway — they share one
bucket, which no value here changes.

---

## 2026-10-03 · Three mail servers are added, and Mailu waits for a fixed release

### DEC-048

- **Decision:** decided 2026-10-03 · refines DEC-045 · area: catalogue
- **Implementation:** implemented → apps/stalwart (#219), apps/docker-mailserver (#220), apps/mailserver-jeboehm (#221); docs/audits/candidate-evaluation-2026-10-03.md; Mailu held
- **Verification:** n/a — the stacks' evidence is LIFECYCLE.md's

`ROADMAP.md` adds no application while the v1.0 items are open, and the exception
of 2026-09-22 left the hold in place for anything proposed afterwards. Seven mail
servers were proposed and checked the same way. Three are added — a third
deliberate exception of the same kind: it changes nothing v1.0 requires, every
stack lands `scaffolded`, and the hold still applies to anything proposed from here
on.

**Added: Stalwart, docker-mailserver and jeboehm/docker-mailserver.** The repository
had no mail server. The three differ in shape — one binary with its own web
interface, one container configured by files, one container per function with an
administration interface and webmail — so the batch covers three ways of running
mail rather than three variants of one.

**Open source is the entry condition for this list as well.** poste.io and Axigen
are proprietary and are not added.

**Mailu is held, not dropped.** CVE-2026-86008, rated high and published on
2026-09-23, lets an account with the domain-manager role take over administrator
accounts. The fix is on `master`; the newest release, 2024.06.61, does not contain
it, and the maintainers preferred the next release over a backport. A published
advisory with no fixed release is what the verdict *Held* is for. Mailu meets every
other requirement and is revisited when a release carries the fix.

**mailcow is not added.** `netfilter-mailcow` runs `privileged: true`, which the
baseline refuses without an exception path, and upstream's configuration has no
switch that leaves the service out. A stack without it would be a deployment its
upstream does not describe.

**Stalwart's licence is recorded, not resolved here.** The published image is built
with the enterprise feature, so code under the Stalwart Enterprise License v2 is in
it, unlocked only by a licence key. Whether the stack pins that image or one built
here without the feature is decided with the stack; `business/twenty` is the
precedent for the first.

**The stacks wait for two answers from the Traefik review.** SMTP and IMAP are not
HTTP: either each stack publishes its mail ports through an opt-in overlay, or
Traefik routes them through TCP entrypoints with PROXY protocol. And each server
holds its own certificate, from its own ACME client, from Traefik's `acme.json`, or
from files issued outside the proxy. Both questions touch `core/traefik`, which is
why they are settled once, there, rather than three times in three stacks.

Evidence per product, the batch order and the decisions each batch depends on:
[`../docs/audits/candidate-evaluation-2026-10-03.md`](../docs/audits/candidate-evaluation-2026-10-03.md).

## 2026-09-25 · `main` requires twelve checks: the ten jobs and both image-scan jobs

### DEC-070

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-25 (#208, #209) · refines DEC-042 · depends on DEC-043 · area: release
- **Implementation:** implemented → the ruleset on `main` (a GitHub setting, updated 2026-09-25: the ten jobs of ci.yml plus the IaC config scan and the Image CVE scan of trivy.yml, 0 approving reviews, no bypass actor, up to date before merging); docs/standards/ci.md §CI Pipeline and docs/security-verification.md state it; .ai/state.md, .ai/quality-gates.md and .ai/risks.md state the twelve (since 2026-10-30)
- **Verification:** mechanical — GitHub enforces the ruleset on every pull request into `main`; the twelve required-check names, read from the ruleset on 2026-10-30, match the job names

A pull request into `main` passes twelve required checks: the ten jobs of `ci.yml` that
`dev` also requires, plus the two jobs of `trivy.yml`. The image scan runs on every pull
request into `main` — in full when the change can alter what the scan sees (#208) — and
not again on the push that follows the merge, because the branch had to be up to date
(#209); the weekly run covers the CVEs published afterwards. A release pull request from
`dev` cannot land while the image gate is red.

scan reported without blocking, so a CRITICAL finding outside `.trivy-baseline.json`

## 2026-09-24 · `cap_add` and `devices` get exception tables

### DEC-047

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-24 (#201) · refines DEC-001 · area: hardening
- **Implementation:** implemented → scripts/ci/check-baseline.py (`CAP_BASELINE`, `CAP_ADD_EXCEPTIONS`, `DEVICE_EXCEPTIONS`; `cap_add: ALL` fails without an exception path)
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_check_baseline.py (both rules; the exception path does not extend to `cap_add: ALL`)

The candidate evaluation attached one decision to batches N, Q, R and S: where
monitoring collectors get host access, and whether `cap_add` and `devices` get an
exception table beside `HOST_MODE_EXCEPTIONS`. The first half was answered in each
batch. The second was raised three times while those stacks were built and settled
in none of them, which is why it is recorded separately here.

The gap was real. `check-baseline.py` enforced `privileged`, the Docker socket,
host networking and the host PID namespace — and nothing about capabilities or
devices. A service could carry `cap_drop: ALL` beside `SYS_RAWIO` and a read-write
`/dev/sda` and pass every gate without a word. `monitoring/scrutiny`'s collector
overlay does exactly that, deliberately and documented in its README, but the
checker had no opinion either way.

**Three rules now.** `cap_add: ALL` fails outright and has no exception path, for
the reason `privileged: true` has none: written under a `cap_drop: ALL` it reads as
hardened and is the opposite. A capability outside `CAP_BASELINE` warns until the
service is listed in `CAP_ADD_EXCEPTIONS`. Any `devices:` entry warns until the
service is listed in `DEVICE_EXCEPTIONS`. Both tables carry the same three fields
as every other exception table.

**`CAP_BASELINE` is six capabilities**, not an arbitrary allow-list. Five of them —
`CHOWN`, `DAC_OVERRIDE`, `FOWNER`, `SETGID`, `SETUID` — are one pattern: an
entrypoint that takes ownership of its data directory and drops to its own user.
They reach no further than the container's own filesystem and namespaces, and they
appear in over a hundred services here, so warning on them would train the reader
to ignore the warning. `NET_BIND_SERVICE` is the sixth for a different reason: it
permits binding a port below 1024 and nothing else, which is narrower than running
the process as root to reach the same result.

The repository needed five exception entries and no compose change, which is the
outcome that made the rule worth adding rather than a rule that would have forced
a rewrite: Collabora's `MKNOD` for its per-document jail, Dify's `SYS_CHROOT` for
the sandbox that isolates user code, Scrutiny's `SYS_RAWIO` and `/dev/sda`, and
cAdvisor's read-only `/dev/kmsg`.

`scripts/ci/test_check_baseline.py` covers both rules, including that the
exception path does not extend to `cap_add: ALL` and that a baseline capability
does not mask an unlisted one beside it. The checker had no tests before.

## 2026-09-24 · Neither Suricata nor Coraza becomes a stack

### DEC-046

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-24 (#200) · area: threat-detection
- **Implementation:** implemented → core/crowdsec/docs/appsec.md (Coraza is the AppSec engine; the CRS collections and why they stay uninstalled by default); ROADMAP.md §Added — the held candidates; no stack for either
- **Verification:** n/a — Suricata's two measurements (the cost under inspection, the false-positive load) wait for a disposable host

The candidate list held two capabilities rather than two applications, each with a
condition attached. Both conditions were tested, and the answer in each case was a
stack that should not be built.

**Coraza.** The condition was a maintained Traefik integration. It is not met —
Coraza's own README lists the WASM extension as "experimental, needs a maintainer",
its newest release is v0.3.0 from 2024-10-29, and Traefik's native integration is
part of the commercial Traefik Hub. The more useful finding is that the question was
already answered: CrowdSec's AppSec engine *is* Coraza, and the OWASP Core Rule Set
installs as the hub collections `crowdsecurity/crs` and `crowdsecurity/crs-inband`.
A reader asking for a Coraza WAF with the Core Rule Set needed documentation, not
software. That gap is closed in `../core/crowdsec/docs/appsec.md`, which also records
why the CRS collections stay uninstalled by default: the rule files CrowdSec serves
still identify as `OWASP_CRS/4.0.0-rc1` while the project's current release is
v4.29.0.

A second WAF inline would also have been a loss rather than a gain — each request
evaluated twice, false positives from two rule sets, and a block with two possible
origins to diagnose.

**Suricata.** Two of the four open questions now have answers, and both narrow
rather than settle the case. Inspecting payloads on a single Docker host means
capturing the bridges, because the physical interface carries TLS to Traefik — so
the traffic examined is decrypted user traffic between the proxy and each
application. And `crowdsecurity/suricata` bans a source on a single severity-1
alert, which turns a passive IDS into an enforcing one; the alerts reach CrowdSec
without that scenario or not at all.

The remaining two — the cost under deep packet inspection and the false-positive
load — need a host that can be flooded and misconfigured without consequence.
Measuring them on a host carrying live services is not an option, so the stack
waits rather than shipping on estimates. When it comes it is passive only: an
inline IPS drops traffic when the engine is down, the failure mode this blueprint
avoids everywhere else.

**What would change each answer.** For Coraza, a maintained Traefik extension with
a current release. For Suricata, a disposable host — at which point the two
measurements are a day's work, and a `HOST_MODE_EXCEPTIONS` entry and a `core/`
stack follow.

kind: it changes nothing v1.0 requires, every stack lands `scaffolded`, the batches
follow the order in the evaluation, and the hold still applies to anything proposed

**Open source is the entry condition for this list.** A product whose deployed code

**obot is added with its Docker API access documented as a deviation**, as Hawser's
direct socket mount is: creating the containers obot runs is root-equivalent on the
host, and the stack says so. A socket proxy sits in front of it: a read-only
allow-list was tried first and does not work — obot calls `ContainerCreate`,
`ContainerRemove`, `ImagePull` and `VolumeCreate` — so the proxy allows those and

**Two products proposed the same day were checked the same way.** paperless-gpt is
added. paperless-ai stays a candidate: its README states that the repository is not
maintained, and it is revisited once the announced rewrite is released or
maintenance resumes.

## 2026-09-20 · Image findings are recorded as facts, and the shipped access default follows them

### DEC-043

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-20 · answers stab C1 · area: updates
- **Implementation:** partial → scripts/ci/trivy-gate.py and .trivy-baseline.json exist (#157, #207, #250); the per-image facts file, the `Exposure` field in UPSTREAM.md and the checker that refuses `access-public` for a restricted stack do not (.ai/tasks.md §1)
- **Verification:** mechanical — the Image CVE scan job on pull requests into main, required there since 2026-09-25 (#208, #209); 109 recorded CRITICAL pairs are unassessed (#249)

The Trivy image scan blocks nothing (`--exit-code 0`), and the last full scan found
1003 CRITICAL findings across 59 of 99 images, all with a published fix. Almost all sit
in the operating-system layer or in bundled components of the image as upstream
publishes it — Perl, libc headers, GnuTLS, ImageMagick, Chromium. The blueprint does not
build those images, so the question is not how to fix them but how to record and handle
them.

**Facts, not a grade.** Each image gets recorded facts: CRITICAL and HIGH counts, how
many have a fix, the age of the release, the scan date, and licence limits where they
exist (a commercial edition with a user cap is a licence fact, not a security one). The
existing dimensions — owner, origin, licence — already work this way and the
sovereignty report is explicit that it is not a score; this is a third set beside them.
Wording on the site names findings in the image as published and passes no judgement on
the project.

**The facts drive one thing: the shipped default.** A stack with findings that make it
unsuitable for open exposure ships a restricted access class (`acc-private`,
`acc-tailscale`, or `acc-deny`), and a checker refuses `acc-public` for it. This is the
existing rule that every stack starts restricted, made machine-checked. Counts alone
mislead — a Perl fix in a Postgres image is not an ImageMagick fix in an upload
server — so the judgement of reach is an authored `Exposure` field with a reason, and the
generated facts only suggest the value.

**Handling, in order.** (1) Upstream has a fix: raise the pin, as any upgrade. (2) No fix
yet, but the stack is contained: record the facts and the reason; the Trivy gate then
blocks only findings that are not already recorded. (3) No fix, upstream not reacting,
and the service is exposed: fork or remove. Cal.diY is the precedent for the third step —
it was forked from a project that had been compromised and is hardened in phases
(`apps/caldiy/docs/hardening-plan.md`). The list of steps to build this is in
[`tasks.md`](tasks.md#1-image-findings-as-facts--closes-audit-finding-c1).

**Built and not built, as of 2026-10-15.** The gate exists: `scripts/ci/trivy-gate.py`
fails the scan on a CRITICAL finding absent from `.trivy-baseline.json`, which records
the accepted findings per image repository. The per-image facts file, the `Exposure`
field in `UPSTREAM.md`, the checker that refuses `acc-public` for a restricted stack
and the catalogue page do not exist; `tasks.md` §1 lists them open.

## 2026-09-20 · No approving-review gate while there is one maintainer

### DEC-042

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-20 · area: release
- **Implementation:** implemented → the rulesets on `main` and `dev` (0 approving reviews, no bypass actor, required checks, up to date before merging), which are GitHub settings rather than files; docs/standards/commit-rules.md §Branch Model describes them; the entry's "ten on main" is twelve since 2026-09-25 (#208, #209)
- **Verification:** mechanical — GitHub enforces both rulesets on every pull request

**Decided.** While this repository has a single maintainer:

- `required_approving_review_count` stays **0** on both protected branches;
- the required CI checks stay enforced — ten on `dev` and ten on `main`;
- the rulesets keep **no bypass actor**, so a red check blocks the owner too;
- no approval rule is introduced that the sole author cannot satisfy;
- the requirement is revisited when a second maintainer exists.

Both branches are governed by rulesets rather than classic branch protection, and
both also require the branch to be up to date before merging.

With a single maintainer a required review has only two shapes, and neither is worth
having. GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so a required
review plus no bypass means nothing can ever merge; a required review with a bypass
means the rule is bypassed on every single merge. The second is what would raise the
OpenSSF Scorecard Branch-Protection check from 3 to 6 — a score describing a rule
nobody honours.

The ceiling is not reachable anyway: Scorecard's tier 4 requires **two** reviewers,
so 10/10 is out of reach for a single-maintainer repository regardless of
configuration. Recorded so the question is not reopened expecting a different answer.
Revisit when a second maintainer exists — that is the condition that changes it, not
the score.

## 2026-09-19 · Personal data on the public site

### DEC-041

- **Decision:** direction (explicitly "not yet a decision") · answers stab D3 (recommendation: adopt the encrypted module; whether an unresolved D3 blocks v1.0 is undecided, ROADMAP.md "decision pending") · area: site
- **Implementation:** not started → site/src/content/docs/legal/index.md, site/src/content/docs/privacy/index.md, site/astro.config.mjs, site/src/data/site-config.ts
- **Verification:** n/a
- **Inputs:** stabilization audit W7 / D3

**Status: direction, not yet a decision.** Summary in [`../ROADMAP.md`](../ROADMAP.md#a-public-repository-should-not-carry-personal-data); the full reasoning is here.

The legal notice and the privacy statement hold a name, a postal address and an
e-mail. The repository is public and meant to be forked, so those values travel
with every copy.

The case to prevent is not someone taking them deliberately. It is the fork
that builds and goes live without anyone looking — and then a stranger's site
carries the original author's legal notice, and the people who read it write to
that author about a site they have nothing to do with. Nobody had to act in bad
faith for that to happen.

Beyond the nuisance, a template that anyone can fork and build ought to be free
of its author's identity by construction. Keeping personal data out of a
public, copyable artefact is both the cleaner engineering answer and the correct
one under data-protection law.

**Direction, not yet a decision.** Encrypt the pages that carry personal data,
commit the ciphertext, and ship a placeholder in their place. What is secret is
the key, not the file: the repository holds a blob anyone can copy and nobody
can read, and a fork inherits a template that visibly asks for its own details.
It still builds on the first try, because the placeholder is a valid page.

`age` looks like the right size: one binary, no keyring, no web of trust, no
expiry, and a key pair that is two lines of text. SOPS earns its place when
single fields inside a YAML stay readable, which is not the case here — whole
files are encrypted, so it would be one layer over the same age. A repository
secret alone will not do either: a secret holds a value, so the imprint would
become an unversioned blob in a form field instead of a file with a history and
a diff.

Two key holders, both able to decrypt:

| Where | Holds |
|---|---|
| GitHub Actions secret | the key the deploy uses, decrypting into the runner's own workspace |
| a password manager | the same key for local editing, alongside the SSH keys already kept there |

An offline backup recipient belongs in the recipients file as well, so a lost
laptop does not take the imprint with it.

**Scope: everything personal, not only the two legal pages.** A fork inherits
the name and address in the legal notice, the contact address in
`security.txt`, the domain in `astro.config.mjs`, and the repository URLs in
the footer and the reference lists. Encrypting the imprint alone would still
leave a stranger's site pointing at this one.

**A fork builds, with the fields empty.** The placeholder is a valid page that
visibly asks for its own details, so nobody has to fix anything before the
first build succeeds.

That works for prose. It does not work for every value: the site URL feeds the
canonical tags and the sitemap, and an empty one produces a broken build rather
than an obvious gap. Values the build needs get a neutral placeholder —
`example.com` and the repository's own URL — while name, address and e-mail go
empty. The distinction is between a field a reader should notice is blank and a
value the build cannot do without.

**One data module rather than encrypted pages.** The values live in a single
module the pages and the config import. `site.ts` is committed and holds the
placeholders; `site.local.ts` is decrypted, gitignored, and wins when present.
That is a better shape than encrypting the markdown: one file to encrypt, one
import to resolve, and nothing in the working tree that a fork could mistake
for its own.

It also dissolves most of the trap. Decrypting over a committed placeholder
invites a thoughtless `git add` that puts real values back into a history that
keeps them; a gitignored file cannot be added by accident. A pre-commit hook
guarding against a forced add is then a belt on top of braces rather than the
only thing standing between the repository and a permanent mistake.

Locally the key never reaches the filesystem, because process substitution
hands `age` a descriptor instead of a path:

    age -d -i <(op read "op://<vault>/<item>/<field>") \
        -o site/src/data/site.local.ts secrets/site.age

The runner needs the same care for the opposite reason: writing the key to a
file and deleting it afterwards leaves a window, however short, so the key
should reach `age` on a descriptor there too.

This concerns the site. The rule that no secret-management tooling belongs in
the blueprint itself stands: no stack gains a dependency, and none of this is
offered to an operator as a way to hold their own credentials.

## 2026-09-19 · Optional watchdogs for the Docker daemon and Traefik, bounded and opt-in

### DEC-040

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-19 (#111) · area: host
- **Implementation:** implemented → core/host-watchdog/ (docker-daemon-watchdog.sh and its units), core/traefik/ops/scripts/traefik-watchdog.sh with its unit examples; both opt-in, listed in core/host-watchdog/ops/host-files.manifest and core/traefik/ops/host-files.manifest (DEC-058)
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/test_host_files.py renders the manifests · open — "Neither script has run on a live host" (the entry)

A read-only host-resilience evaluation found that `restart: unless-stopped` and
container healthchecks already cover a crashed process, but nothing acts on a
service that is running and unhealthy — Traefik included — or on the Docker
daemon's API hanging while the process stays alive. `docker inspect --format
'{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.RestartCount}}'` in `docs/resource-measurement.md` was
already a manual command, never automated.

`willfarrell/autoheal`, the common general-purpose answer, was already rejected
once in this repository — `business/openproject/docker-compose.yml` omits it
because it needs a direct `docker.sock` mount, which containers here do not get.
A host-installed script run by systemd as root is a different trust boundary and
does not need that exception; it has the access an administrator already has.

Two independent scripts, `core/host-watchdog/docker-daemon-watchdog.sh` and
`core/traefik/ops/scripts/traefik-watchdog.sh`, each follow the same bounded
model: N consecutive confirmed failures → one recovery attempt → re-verify →
report and stop retrying if it did not hold. Neither installs by default,
neither is required by anything else, and either can be enabled alone. Both
report to a Healthchecks check on every run — the same dead-man's-switch
pattern `backup/borgmatic` already uses — so the watchdog itself going silent
is caught independently of whatever it watches.

Restarting Traefik on sustained unhealthy status is accepted specifically
because it holds no state — a wrong restart costs seconds of routing, not
data. This is not a general auto-heal policy: a stateful service reported
unhealthy should still alert a person, not restart itself, and the README
says so explicitly.

Neither script has run on a live host. The systemd hardening blocks mirror
`backup/borgmatic.service.example`'s pattern as a documented starting point,
not a verified one — matching this repository's own standard for anything
new: configured, not yet exercised.

## 2026-09-19 · Dify and Langfuse keep their real component count

### DEC-039

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-19 (#117) · area: catalogue
- **Implementation:** implemented → apps/dify (ten services), monitoring/langfuse (six)
- **Verification:** n/a — the stacks' evidence is LIFECYCLE.md's; the MinIO image withdrawal is recorded in monitoring/langfuse/README.md and UPSTREAM.md (#206)

Dify is ten services and Langfuse six, and none was collapsed: the worker, plugin
daemon, sandbox and SSRF proxy are what makes Dify's chat, knowledge-base and code
paths work, and Langfuse v4's ClickHouse, Redis and MinIO are all in its read and
write path. Where a component is optional upstream it was left out and named in
`UPSTREAM.md`: nginx and certbot (Traefik replaces them), workflow collaboration
and the 1.17 Agent runtime (backend, local sandbox, second proxy).

Dify's vector store is pgvector, not Weaviate and not the repository's own Qdrant:
Dify supports several, and no stack here embeds another. Langfuse sits in
`monitoring/` because it receives traces, and nothing else in the repository sends
to it or depends on it.

Exceptions were measured, not assumed. The plugin daemon ships as root but runs as
uid 1001, read-only, with installs verified. The sandbox needs five capabilities
(each removal broke a code run; a sixth was not needed). Squid stays root with five
capabilities. Langfuse's web service needs a 2 GB limit and a raised Node heap or it
loops at start, and both Node services bind to the container's hostname address, not
loopback, so their healthchecks call `$(hostname)`. Dify's licence and Open WebUI's
are classed source-available in the sovereignty report.

## 2026-09-19 · The AI gateways and chat UI are independent stacks

### DEC-038

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-19 (#116) · area: catalogue
- **Implementation:** implemented → apps/litellm, apps/open-webui, apps/agentgateway (the backend is configuration; the READMEs say so instead of wiring a shared network)
- **Verification:** n/a — the stacks' evidence is LIFECYCLE.md's

`apps/litellm`, `apps/open-webui` and `apps/agentgateway` were added without a
dependency between them or on the foundation stacks. Each takes its backend as
configuration (an OpenAI-compatible URL) and ships pointing at an Ollama address
that only resolves if the operator has one; the READMEs say so instead of wiring
a shared network.

Three secrets findings shaped the stacks. LiteLLM and Open WebUI have no `_FILE`
variants, so each carries an `entrypoint.sh` that exports Docker Secrets;
agentgateway's image is distroless and has no shell, so its client key is stored
in the config only as a SHA-256 hash and its UI login is an htpasswd file mounted
as a secret. Open WebUI runs as an unprivileged uid though its image defaults to
root, and creates its administrator from the environment because upstream
otherwise makes the first registrant the administrator. agentgateway's default
binds metrics to all interfaces; the template pins them to loopback.

Open WebUI's licence is BSD-3-Clause with a branding-preservation clause, so the
sovereignty report classes it as source-available rather than OSI.

## 2026-09-18 · The AI foundation exists; vLLM is documented as unverified on GPU

### DEC-037

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-18 (#109) · supersedes DEC-032.a · area: catalogue
- **Implementation:** implemented → apps/ollama, apps/vllm, apps/qdrant; docs/architecture.md §AI & Local AI is deployment, not engineering; ROADMAP.md §Out of scope here narrowed
- **Verification:** n/a — the stacks' evidence is LIFECYCLE.md's; vLLM's CUDA image has not run on a GPU (apps/vllm/README.md)

The 2026-09 position that AI & Local AI stays latent was conditional: it waited
on a deployment somebody needs. That need was declared, and `apps/ollama`,
`apps/vllm` and `apps/qdrant` landed together. `docs/architecture.md` now says
deploying and hardening AI services is this repository's job and the
engineering above them is not; `ROADMAP.md`'s out-of-scope entry narrowed to
match. The earlier decision below stays as the record of why the absence was
reasoned.

Ollama and vLLM are both kept although both serve models — the repository
carries alternatives deliberately — because they serve different deployments.

Two decisions about evidence. vLLM's CUDA image is 8.7 GB and needs a GPU, and
the test host had neither the disk nor the hardware. The stack was therefore
validated on the CPU build of the same release — real inference, the
authentication behaviour, the Traefik path allowlist, the hardening flags — and
says in its README and `UPSTREAM.md` that the CUDA image has not run and that
its non-root and read-only settings are a first-run hypothesis for it, not a
result. And the authentication limits are properties to design around, not to
hide: Ollama has none, vLLM's key covers `/v1` only (`/invocations` runs
inference without it), so vLLM's router forwards `/v1/` only and both READMEs
state that peers on `proxy-public` reach everything.

## 2026-09-18 · Windmill runs without job sandboxing rather than with privileged workers

### DEC-036

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-18 (#108) · area: hardening
- **Implementation:** implemented → apps/windmill/docker-compose.yml (no privileged worker; the comment says why), apps/windmill/UPSTREAM.md, apps/windmill/README.md
- **Verification:** n/a — the stack's evidence is LIFECYCLE.md's; the sandbox retest on bare metal is recorded as open in apps/windmill/UPSTREAM.md

Upstream's default Windmill worker is `privileged: true`, for PID-namespace
isolation of job code. The repository baseline has no exception path for
privileged containers, so the stack does not use it. NSJAIL, upstream's
unprivileged alternative, was tried with `cap_add: SYS_ADMIN`,
`seccomp=unconfined` and `apparmor=unconfined` and still failed on a `mount()`
call; whether that is specific to the nested-virtualisation test host is not
established. The stack therefore ships with no per-job isolation beyond the
worker container's own boundary (non-root, all capabilities dropped,
read-only root filesystem, `no-new-privileges`), and says so in the stack's
README and `UPSTREAM.md` instead of implying a sandbox.

Two smaller consequences. Workers join a per-stack `app-egress` network — the
pattern `apps/nextcloud` and `business/invoiceninja` already use — because
runtime and dependency downloads fail on `app-internal` alone. And a fresh
Windmill carries a published superadmin password, so the router defaults to
`acc-deny` until `ops/bootstrap-admin.sh` has replaced it. The first
reproducible retest is on a bare-metal host, where NSJAIL may work.

## 2026-09-18 · A blueprint entry needs an independently operated service, not just a container

### DEC-035

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-18 · area: catalogue
- **Implementation:** implemented (as a rule) → ROADMAP.md §Out of scope here (OCRmyPDF), docs/architecture.md §Document Processing has the capabilities, and one standalone service
- **Verification:** n/a

Clarified while evaluating OCRmyPDF for `apps/`. Functional overlap with an
existing stack is not a reason to exclude a tool — this repository already
carries multiple alternatives per category deliberately (dashboards, photo
galleries, scheduling) and continues to. The separate, narrower test is
whether a tool is something to deploy, harden and operate as its own service
at all: a pure CLI utility or job that upstream itself runs as one container
per invocation does not become more of a service by wrapping it in Compose.

`apps/docling-serve` passes this test — an API with its own healthcheck,
authentication and multiple plausible independent callers. OCRmyPDF does not:
upstream's own documentation describes its Docker image as ephemeral, "one
OCR job and terminates, just like a command line program... as opposed to the
more conventional case, where a Docker container runs as a server." No
`apps/ocrmypdf` entry was created, and none is planned as a substitute — the
need this would have filled was never established as real, so there is
nothing to replace it with. Recorded in `ROADMAP.md` → "Out of scope here" so
the absence is not silently re-proposed later.

Tika, Gotenberg and ClamAV were explicitly held out of this batch by the same
correction that sharpened the criterion above — an earlier plan had scoped
standalone Tika and Gotenberg stacks into this batch alongside `docling-serve`,
before that plan was implemented. They remain embedded in Paperless-ngx /
optional in Seafile-Pro, unchanged, pending a later evaluation.

## 2026-09-18 · `development/` becomes a Supporting-tier domain

### DEC-034

- **Decision:** decided 2026-09-18 (#106) · refines DEC-005, DEC-027 · area: architecture
- **Implementation:** implemented → development/ (static-site, web-api, each proven by a minimal fixture); scripts/ci/check-structure.py `ROOTS` and `EXCEPT_DIRS`; docs/architecture.md §Development is a Supporting-tier domain, not a sixth category
- **Verification:** mechanical — scripts/ci/check-structure.py and scripts/ci/check-baseline.py parse both patterns · open — no project has been copied out of development/ and operated (docs/standards/custom-application.md)

The Development / Custom Applications conceptual domain had no physical home:
its two real members, `business/vikunja` and `apps/caldiy`, sit under the
normal five categories, and `docs/standards/custom-application.md` stated that
a genuinely first-party application — source with no upstream — "stays absent
until a real application needs it." That precondition is now met: the need for
a reusable starting point across future first-party projects, not for one
specific named application, was declared real and current.

`development/` is not a sixth entry in the five-category access-pattern table.
The Directory Structure test asks how a running service reaches the system; a
deployment pattern that is never run from this repository has no access
pattern to test. It is a Supporting-tier directory instead, alongside `docs/`,
`scripts/ci/` and `site/` — checked by `scripts/ci/check-structure.py` anyway,
because unlike those three it holds real, buildable compose files. `ROOTS` in
that checker gained `development`, and `development/static-site` and
`development/web-api` were added to `EXCEPT_DIRS` for the same reason
`apps/_reference` is there: a template, not a versioned app, no `UPSTREAM.md`.

Two patterns exist: `development/static-site/` (a build step producing static
files, Astro and Vite/React recipes differing only in the build stage) and
`development/web-api/` (a generic backend, deliberately without a database —
one is added the way `apps/_reference` shows, only when a real application
needs one). Each is proven by a minimal fixture: a real `docker compose build
&& up`, hardened (`read_only`, `cap_drop: ALL`, non-root), reporting healthy.
The fixture proves the pattern's contract, not that a real project has been
through it — no project has yet been copied out of `development/` and
operated, and `custom-application.md` records that as a standing gap rather
than closing it.

`docs/architecture.md`'s "Development is a mission scope, not the local
test-stack mode" section is now "Development is a Supporting-tier domain, not
a sixth category", and `custom-application.md` gained this as a third shape
alongside the in-repo build layer and the external governed pipeline.

Third-party developer tooling (Mailpit, GreenMail, Adminer, IT-Tools, Whoami,
Windmill) is unaffected — it stays in `apps/` under the ordinary
categorisation test and is linked from `development/README.md`, which does not
become a stack listing.
